Condition: Eye foreign body and corneal abrasion (includes chemical splash to the eye) (eye-foreign-body-abrasion)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.722 probability of at least one event per crew member, 6 month LEO mission, 1 EVA (IMM model output)
severity: 3 (can threaten sight; eye chemical burn is a modeled evacuation driver)
quote: EYE ABRASION (FOREIGN BODY) 7.22E-01
regions: head

Condition: Eye foreign body and corneal abrasion (includes chemical splash to the eye) (eye-foreign-body-abrasion)
red flags: Object stuck in the eye; any chemical in the eye; any change in vision (blurred or double); eye painful and red; nausea or headache with eye pain; bleeding that will not stop

Condition: Eye foreign body and corneal abrasion (includes chemical splash to the eye) (eye-foreign-body-abrasion)
tests possible onboard: Pain score (painScore); visual acuity each eye with the ISS eye chart (no equipment id, not in equipment.json); no fluorescein or slit lamp step for a layperson found
rank: 1
rank reason: High likelihood plus a sight threat; floating debris is the most recorded eye event on Shuttle and ISS.

Condition: Eye foreign body and corneal abrasion (includes chemical splash to the eye) (eye-foreign-body-abrasion)
plain: Something in your eye or a scratch on it. Do not rub it. Chemicals or a stuck object are an emergency.
severity basis quote: In one assessment, Eye Chemical Burn was the top influential medical condition contributing to the probability of evacuation for certain ISS mission conditions

Condition: Eye foreign body and corneal abrasion (includes chemical splash to the eye) (eye-foreign-body-abrasion)
red flags quote: There appears to be a scratch, cut, or something has gone into (penetrated) the eyeball.

Condition: Eye foreign body and corneal abrasion (includes chemical splash to the eye) (eye-foreign-body-abrasion)
notes: Meer 2023 reports 70 of 104 ocular events in LSAH records were eye abrasion from a foreign body (Shuttle and ISS to Expedition 13). Supporting quote (Meer;): "There were 70 corneal abrasions, 4 dry eyes, 4 eye debris, 5 complaints of ocular irritation, 6 chemical burns"

Condition: Space motion sickness (space adaptation) (space-motion-sickness)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.730 probability per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM); OCHMO brief says up to 73% of crew in first 2-3 days
severity: 2 (can stop work; vomiting causes dehydration; EVA delayed)
quote: SPACE MOTION SICKNESS (SA) 7.30E-01
regions: head|abdomen

Condition: Space motion sickness (space adaptation) (space-motion-sickness)
red flags: More than 2 vomiting episodes; symptoms beyond 72 hours; clear drop in performance; cannot keep fluids down; blood or coffee-ground material in vomit
tests possible onboard: heartRate and BP (eq-bp-monitor, eq-manual-pulse); temperatureC (eq-thermometer-oral); electrolytes if vomiting (eq-pcba-istat, EC6+ cartridge); auscultation (eq-stethoscope)
rank: 2

Condition: Space motion sickness (space adaptation) (space-motion-sickness)
rank reason: Most common early-flight problem; vomiting in a closed cabin or suit and dehydration make it more than a nuisance.
plain: Feeling sick from weightlessness. Keep your head still. Vomiting many times is serious.
severity basis quote: Concerns include health decrements (dehydration and weakness) and decreased crew performance.

Condition: Space motion sickness (space adaptation) (space-motion-sickness)
red flags quote: includes more than 2 episodes of vomiting; significant performance decrement may be apparent; symptoms may persist beyond 72 hours

Condition: Space motion sickness (space adaptation) (space-motion-sickness)
notes: MTB-004 p4 lists diagnosis capabilities: auscultation device and blood analysis (check electrolytes if vomiting). Supporting quote (OCHMO-MTB-004 Rev A;): "Capabilities needed for diagnosis: Auscultation device, blood analysis (check electrolytes if vomiting)"

Condition: Headache in flight (space adaptation, late, and CO2-induced) (headache-co2)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Late headache 0.592, space adaptation headache 0.351, CO2-induced headache 0.306 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 2 (usually not dangerous; CO2 headache signals a cabin air problem for all crew; some red flags mean stroke or bleeding in the brain)
quote: HEADACHE (LATE) 5.92E-01
regions: head

Condition: Headache in flight (space adaptation, late, and CO2-induced) (headache-co2)
red flags: Sudden explosive headache; worst headache ever; slurred speech, vision change, weakness, loss of balance or confusion; fever with stiff neck; headache after a head injury; headache worse over 24 hours

Condition: Headache in flight (space adaptation, late, and CO2-induced) (headache-co2)
tests possible onboard: painScore; temperatureC (eq-thermometer-oral); systolicBP/diastolicBP/heartRate (eq-bp-monitor); cabin CO2 reading from vehicle sensors (no measurement key exists)
rank: 3
rank reason: Very common, and the card can catch two dangerous things: a CO2 problem that affects everyone, and rare brain emergencies.

Condition: Headache in flight (space adaptation, late, and CO2-induced) (headache-co2)
plain: Headache is common in space. A sudden, very bad headache, or trouble speaking or seeing, is an emergency.
severity basis quote: Headaches at levels between 2.8-4.5 mmHg; worsening with increasing levels of CO2 accompanied by fatigue and malaise flushing.

Condition: Headache in flight (space adaptation, late, and CO2-induced) (headache-co2)
red flags quote: Your headache comes on suddenly and is explosive or violent. This kind of headache needs medical attention right away.

Condition: Headache in flight (space adaptation, late, and CO2-induced) (headache-co2)
notes: van Oosterhout 2024: 22 of 24 ISS astronauts had at least one headache in flight. TB-004: 19 of 49 astronauts reported headaches in an ISS CO2 study. Supporting quote (OCHMO-TB-004 Rev D;): "19 of the 49 astronauts reported experiencing headaches (~38.7%)."

Condition: Choking or obstructed airway (choking-airway)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.0533 probability per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 3 (life threat within minutes)
quote: CHOKING/OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY 5.33E-02
regions: head|chest
red flags: Cannot speak; difficulty breathing; noisy or high-pitched breathing; weak cough; bluish skin; becomes unresponsive

Condition: Choking or obstructed airway (choking-airway)
tests possible onboard: oxygenSat (eq-blood-oximeter); heartRate (eq-manual-pulse). Microgravity method for back blows or abdominal thrusts: NOT FOUND (searched OCHMO briefs, HRP 2017 evidence report, Hinkelbein 2020)
rank: 4
rank reason: Rare but kills in minutes, so the ground cannot help in time; the card must stand alone.
plain: If they cannot talk or breathe, act now. Do not wait for the ground.

Condition: Choking or obstructed airway (choking-airway)
severity basis quote: Loss of consciousness (unresponsiveness) if the blockage is not cleared
red flags quote: look for these danger signs: Inability to speak Difficulty breathing
notes: Earth first aid assumes gravity and a standing rescuer. Microgravity technique not found in public sources.

Condition: Fire, smoke inhalation and burns (fire-smoke-burns)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Smoke inhalation 0.0112, burns secondary to fire 0.00526 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM; model-derived, not observed events)
severity: 3 (immediate threat to whole crew)
quote: SMOKE INHALATION 1.12E-02
regions: chest|head|skin
red flags: Breathed in smoke; burn the size of a palm or larger; full-thickness burn; burn from chemicals or electricity; signs of shock

Condition: Fire, smoke inhalation and burns (fire-smoke-burns)
tests possible onboard: oxygenSat (eq-blood-oximeter); heartRate and BP (eq-bp-monitor); painScore. Pulse oximeter accuracy after smoke: NOT FOUND in sources read
rank: 5
rank reason: Low modeled probability but a whole-crew life threat; brief lists fire and toxic atmosphere as always required.
plain: Fire or smoke: get clean air first. Then check burns and breathing.

Condition: Fire, smoke inhalation and burns (fire-smoke-burns)
severity basis quote: combustion products can present an immediate threat to the life of the crew due to the limited escape options
red flags quote: The person breathed in smoke.

Condition: Fire, smoke inhalation and burns (fire-smoke-burns)
notes: IMM report p1: fire, smoke and ammonia incidence come from the ISS Fire Model, not actual in-flight events. Supporting quote (Ranking of Medical Conditions by Probability (NASA IMM Data Request Report;): "Incidence rates of Burns Secondary to Fire, Smoke Inhalation, and Toxic Exposure: Ammonia are derived from the ISS Fire Model"

Condition: Skin abrasion, laceration and bleeding (bleeding-laceration-abrasion)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Skin abrasion 0.821, skin laceration 0.0181 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 2 (3 if bleeding cannot be controlled)
quote: SKIN ABRASION 8.21E-01
regions: skin|leftArm|rightArm|leftLeg|rightLeg|head

Condition: Skin abrasion, laceration and bleeding (bleeding-laceration-abrasion)
red flags: Bleeding cannot be controlled; wound may need stitches; dirt cannot be cleaned out; signs of internal bleeding or shock; signs of infection
tests possible onboard: heartRate, systolicBP (eq-bp-monitor); painScore; temperatureC for infection (eq-thermometer-oral)
rank: 6
rank reason: Second most likely event in the model; severe bleeding is on the brief always-list.

Condition: Skin abrasion, laceration and bleeding (bleeding-laceration-abrasion)
plain: Press on a bleeding cut. If it will not stop, it is an emergency.
severity basis quote: You think there may be internal bleeding or shock.
red flags quote: Bleeding can't be controlled, it required the use of a tourniquet, or it was caused by a serious injury.
notes: Behavior of free-floating blood in microgravity: NOT FOUND in sources read.

Condition: Skin rash, allergic reaction and anaphylaxis (allergy-anaphylaxis)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Skin rash 0.821, allergic reaction (mild to moderate) 0.182, anaphylaxis 0.000245 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 3 for anaphylaxis; 1 for rash
quote: Anaphylaxis 2.45E-04
regions: skin|head|chest

Condition: Skin rash, allergic reaction and anaphylaxis (allergy-anaphylaxis)
red flags: Difficulty breathing, wheeze or high-pitched breathing; swelling of face, eyes or tongue; very hoarse or whispered voice; dizziness; unconsciousness
tests possible onboard: oxygenSat (eq-blood-oximeter); heartRate, systolicBP (eq-bp-monitor)
rank: 7
rank reason: Rash is the most reported ISS event; anaphylaxis is rare but fatal fast and is on the brief always-list.

Condition: Skin rash, allergic reaction and anaphylaxis (allergy-anaphylaxis)
plain: A rash is common. Swelling of the face or trouble breathing is an emergency.
severity basis quote: Anaphylaxis is an emergency condition that needs medical attention right away.
red flags quote: A warning sign of dangerous throat swelling is a very hoarse or whispered voice, or coarse sounds when the person is breathing in air.

Condition: Skin rash, allergic reaction and anaphylaxis (allergy-anaphylaxis)
notes: Crucian 2016: skin rashes were the most reported event at 1.12 per flight year in 46 ISS long-duration crew. Supporting quote (Crucian et al. 2016;): "Skin rashes were the most reported event (1.12/flight year)"

Condition: Back pain (space adaptation) and back injury (back-pain-injury)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Space adaptation back pain 0.525, back injury 0.443 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM); 52% in first 2-5 days (OCHMO)
severity: 1 for adaptation back pain; 2 for injury
quote: BACK PAIN (SA) 5.25E-01
regions: spine

Condition: Back pain (space adaptation) and back injury (back-pain-injury)
red flags: Loss of control of urine or stool; weakness or numbness in buttocks, thigh, leg or pelvis; pain after a hard blow; fever with back pain; pain down the leg below the knee
tests possible onboard: painScore; temperatureC (eq-thermometer-oral)
rank: 8
rank reason: Very common; card is mostly reassurance plus spinal red flags.

Condition: Back pain (space adaptation) and back injury (back-pain-injury)
plain: Back ache is common early in flight. Numb legs or losing bladder control is an emergency.
severity basis quote: Positioning exercises, analgesic medications, and exercise are used to manage symptoms with ≥85% pain relief effectiveness for all treatments
red flags quote: Loss of control over urine or stool (incontinence)

Condition: Back pain (space adaptation) and back injury (back-pain-injury)
notes: MTB-004 p3: SABP occurs in 52% of space travelers during the first 2-5 days of flight (Kerstman 2012). Supporting quote (OCHMO-MTB-004 Rev A;): "Space Adaptation Back Pain (SABP) occurs in 52% of space travelers during the first 2-5 days of flight."

Condition: Urinary retention and urinary tract infection (urinary-retention-uti)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Urinary retention 0.00697 (male) and 0.0556 (female); UTI 0.0811 (male) and 0.490 (female) per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 2 (3 if infection spreads; urosepsis is a modeled evacuation driver)
quote: URINARY RETENTION (SA) 6.97E-03
regions: abdomen
red flags: Cannot pass urine; fever; back or side pain; blood in urine

Condition: Urinary retention and urinary tract infection (urinary-retention-uti)
tests possible onboard: Urine Chemstrip (eq-urine-chemstrip); temperatureC (eq-thermometer-oral); painScore
rank: 9
rank reason: Documented in flight and needs a catheter skill; untreated it can lead to sepsis.
plain: Not able to pee, or burning when you pee. Fever with it is serious.
severity basis quote: with sepsis (urosepsis as primary driver) being the third

Condition: Urinary retention and urinary tract infection (urinary-retention-uti)
red flags quote: there is a possibility of performance impact during spaceflight due to significant discomfort from urinary retention and associated UTI

Condition: Urinary retention and urinary tract infection (urinary-retention-uti)
notes: MTB-003 p8: 9 cases of urinary retention documented in flight, 16 if suggestive symptoms are included. Supporting quote (OCHMO-MTB-003 Rev A;): "9 cases of urinary retention have been documented in-flight, 16 total if symptoms suggestive of urinary retention are included."

Condition: Decompression sickness after EVA (decompression-sickness)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.0116 per crew member, 6 month LEO with 1 EVA (IMM); rises with EVA count
severity: 3 (can be catastrophic)
quote: Decompression Sickness Secondary to EVA 1.16E-02
regions: leftArm|rightArm|leftLeg|rightLeg|chest|head|skin
red flags: Joint pain after EVA or pressure change; stroke-like symptoms; loss of consciousness; seizure; cough and shortness of breath

Condition: Decompression sickness after EVA (decompression-sickness)
tests possible onboard: oxygenSat (eq-blood-oximeter); heartRate, BP (eq-bp-monitor); painScore
rank: 10
rank reason: Tied to a planned activity, can be catastrophic, and needs a fast specific response.
plain: New joint pain or numbness after a spacewalk can be the bends. Tell the ground right away.

Condition: Decompression sickness after EVA (decompression-sickness)
severity basis quote: it can lead to musculoskeletal pain, neurological impairment, cardiopulmonary compromise, cognitive impairment, risk to mission outcomes/success, and death
red flags quote: acute, severe symptoms such as stroke-like neurological, loss of consciousness, seizures, cardiac ischemia
notes: IMM report p1 says DCS incidence may differ for exploration missions.

Condition: Kidney stone (nephrolithiasis) (kidney-stone)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.00182 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM); OCHMO: second most likely reason for ISS medical evacuation
severity: 3 (evacuation driver)
quote: Nephrolithiasis 1.82E-03
regions: abdomen|spine
red flags: Severe back or side pain that will not go away; blood in urine; fever and chills; vomiting; cloudy or bad-smelling urine

Condition: Kidney stone (nephrolithiasis) (kidney-stone)
tests possible onboard: Urine Chemstrip for blood (eq-urine-chemstrip); temperatureC; painScore; guided ultrasound with AMOS software (not in equipment.json)
rank: 11
rank reason: Low probability but a top evacuation driver, and bone loss in flight raises the risk.
plain: Very bad side or back pain that comes in waves. Tell the ground.

Condition: Kidney stone (nephrolithiasis) (kidney-stone)
severity basis quote: kidney stone is the second most likely reason for emergency medical evacuation from the ISS
red flags quote: Severe pain in your back or side that will not go away
notes: MTB-003 p6: one reported nephrolithiasis episode in flight (a cosmonaut); no USOS crew in-flight stones. Supporting quote (OCHMO-MTB-003 Rev A;): "To date there has been one reported episode of nephrolithiasis during spaceflight"

Condition: Respiratory infection (upper and lower) (respiratory-infection)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.453 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM); upper respiratory symptoms 0.97 per flight year on ISS (Crucian 2016)
severity: 2
quote: RESPIRATORY INFECTION 4.53E-01
regions: chest|head
red flags: Problems breathing; symptoms worse or not better after 7 to 10 days

Condition: Respiratory infection (upper and lower) (respiratory-infection)
tests possible onboard: temperatureC (eq-thermometer-oral); oxygenSat (eq-blood-oximeter); heartRate; auscultation (eq-stethoscope)
rank: 12
rank reason: Common; a low oxygen reading turns it into an emergency.
plain: Cold or chest infection. Trouble breathing or low oxygen is serious.
severity basis quote: followed by upper respiratory symptoms (0.97/flight year)

Condition: Respiratory infection (upper and lower) (respiratory-infection)
red flags quote: You have problems breathing.
notes: Supporting quote (Crucian et al. 2016;): "followed by upper respiratory symptoms (0.97/flight year)"

Condition: Diarrhea and gastroenteritis (diarrhea-gastroenteritis)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Diarrhea 0.453, gastroenteritis 0.0705 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 2 (dehydration)
quote: DIARRHEA 4.53E-01
regions: abdomen
red flags: Signs of dehydration (less urine, dizziness, dry mouth); blood or pus in stool; black stool; belly pain that does not go away; fever

Condition: Diarrhea and gastroenteritis (diarrhea-gastroenteritis)
tests possible onboard: temperatureC; heartRate and BP (eq-bp-monitor); electrolytes (eq-pcba-istat)
rank: 13
rank reason: Common; dehydration risk adds to space fluid shifts.
plain: Loose stools. Drink. Blood in the stool or dizziness is serious.
severity basis quote: Contact your provider right away if you or your child shows signs of dehydration
red flags quote: Blood or pus in your stools

Condition: Joint sprain, muscle strain and fracture (shoulder, elbow, ankle, wrist) (sprain-strain-fracture)
likelihood per mission or per person year: Shoulder sprain/strain 0.340, elbow 0.203, ankle 0.188, wrist fracture 0.00118 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 2
quote: SHOULDER SPRAIN/STRAIN 3.40E-01
regions: leftArm|rightArm|leftLeg|rightLeg
red flags: Possible broken bone; joint out of position; serious injury or severe pain; pop with immediate loss of use

Condition: Joint sprain, muscle strain and fracture (shoulder, elbow, ankle, wrist) (sprain-strain-fracture)
tests possible onboard: painScore; heartRate
rank: 14
rank reason: Exercise and EVA cause these; fracture splinting is on the brief always-list.
plain: Hurt joint. Rest it. A bent or useless limb is serious.
severity basis quote: The joint appears out of position.
red flags quote: You think you have a broken bone

Condition: Joint sprain, muscle strain and fracture (shoulder, elbow, ankle, wrist) (sprain-strain-fracture)
notes: CONFLICT: MTB-006 p7 says no in-flight shoulder injuries have been reported, while the IMM table marks shoulder sprain/strain as having occurred in flight. Needs team review. Supporting quote (OCHMO-MTB-006;): "There are currently no reported incidences of shoulder injuries occurring in-flight."

Condition: Sudden cardiac arrest (CPR in microgravity) (sudden-cardiac-arrest)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.0000075 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: 3 (fatal without CPR in minutes)
quote: Sudden Cardiac Arrest 7.50E-06
regions: chest
red flags: No breathing or only gasping; no pulse; unconscious
tests possible onboard: AED rhythm check (eq-aed); patient restraint (eq-cmrs); heartRate (eq-manual-pulse)
rank: 15

Condition: Sudden cardiac arrest (CPR in microgravity) (sudden-cardiac-arrest)
rank reason: Very rare in the model, but CPR is on the brief always-list and the microgravity method differs from Earth.
plain: Not breathing and no pulse: start chest pushes now.
severity basis quote: In immediate BLS, the chest compression method of choice is the Evetts-Russomano method (ER)
red flags quote: CPR should be done if a person has any of the following symptoms:

Condition: Sudden cardiac arrest (CPR in microgravity) (sudden-cardiac-arrest)
notes: Severity quote is about method, not severity; severity tier is a team judgment (cardiac arrest is fatal without treatment). Supporting quote (Hinkelbein et al. 2020;): "As soon as the patient has been restrained on the Crew Medical Restraint System chest compressions SHOULD be applied using the Handstand-method"

Condition: Late insomnia (late-insomnia)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.912 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: not graded
quote: LATE INSOMNIA 9.12E-01
regions: head
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
rank reason: Most likely condition, but low acute danger; better served by daily sleep tracking than an emergency card.
notes: Considered, not in top 15.

likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.433 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: not graded
quote: BAROTRAUMA (EAR/SINUS BLOCK) 4.33E-01
regions: head
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
rank reason: Common but low consequence.
notes: Considered, not in top 15.

Condition: Nasal congestion (space adaptation) (nasal-congestion)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.586 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: not graded
quote: NASAL CONGESTION (SA) 5.86E-01
regions: head
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
rank reason: Common, low consequence.
notes: Considered, not in top 15.

Condition: Venous thrombosis (including internal jugular vein) (venous-thrombosis)
likelihood per mission or per person year: NOT FOUND as a rate; IMM report table has no VTE row. OCHMO: very small number of crew
severity: not graded
quote: Obstructive thrombi have been identified in a very small number of crewmembers
regions: head|chest|leftLeg|rightLeg
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1

Condition: Venous thrombosis (including internal jugular vein) (venous-thrombosis)
rank reason: Serious and documented (2019 jugular case) but no public rate; candidate for Batch 2.
notes: Considered, not in top 15.

Condition: Angina or myocardial infarction (chest-pain-acs)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.000315 (male), 0.000235 (female) per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: not graded
quote: Angina/Myocardial Infarction 3.15E-04
regions: chest
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
rank reason: Rare; existing team chest card covers the entry point.
notes: Considered, not in top 15.

Condition: Acute radiation syndrome (acute-radiation-syndrome)
likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.00141 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM)
severity: not graded
quote: Acute Radiation Syndrome 1.41E-03
regions: skin|abdomen
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
rank reason: Rare in LEO; higher relevance beyond LEO; covered by section 8.
notes: Considered, not in top 15.

likelihood per mission or per person year: 0.000000725 per crew member, 6 month LEO (IMM; model-derived)
severity: not graded
quote: Toxic Exposure: Ammonia 7.25E-07
regions: chest|head|skin
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
rank reason: Very rare in model; fold into fire and toxic atmosphere card.
notes: Considered, not in top 15.

severity: not graded
quote: Behavioral Emergency 7.15E-06
regions: head
red flags: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1
tests possible onboard: NOT RESEARCHED in Batch 1

painScore in eye-foreign-body-abrasion
researcher note: No vital sign change is described for eye injury in any source read.

quote: NOT FOUND

heartRate in eye-foreign-body-abrasion
researcher note: Looked in: Suh 2025, Meer 2023, MedlinePlus 000054, 2001 ISS eye pages. No vital sign change described. Threshold quote and source are in decisions.md section 3.

heartRate in space-motion-sickness
unit: bpm
expected value or range in condition: May rise if dehydrated: SMS raises dehydration risk, and dehydration can cause a rapid heartbeat (MedlinePlus 000982). No SMS-specific value.
alert threshold: NEWS2 score 3: 40 or below, or 131 or above (decisions.md ref d3a). Earth hospital scale.
direction: high
inflight baseline ref: baselines-inflight.csv rows 3-5

heartRate in space-motion-sickness
spaceflight adjustment: None found: mean 24 h heart rate unchanged in flight (baselines-inflight.csv row 3, Norsk 2015).
quote: Concerns include health decrements (dehydration and weakness) and decreased crew performance.

heartRate in space-motion-sickness
researcher note: Link to heart rate is through dehydration. MedlinePlus Dehydration (000982), Symptoms: "Rapid heartbeat". Pallor and sweating are listed SMS signs (MTB-004 p6) but are not measurement keys. Threshold quote and source are in decisions.md section 3.

systolicBP in space-motion-sickness
unit: mmHg
expected value or range in condition: May fall if dehydrated (low blood pressure is a dehydration sign). No SMS-specific value.
alert threshold: NEWS2 score 3: 90 or below (decisions.md ref d3b). Earth hospital scale.
direction: low
inflight baseline ref: baselines-inflight.csv rows 8, 10, 11

systolicBP in space-motion-sickness
spaceflight adjustment: Resting 24 h systolic about 8 mmHg lower in flight than preflight (baselines-inflight.csv row 8, Norsk 2015). Compare with the crew member's own in-flight baseline.
quote: Blood pressure that drops when you stand up after lying down.

systolicBP in space-motion-sickness
researcher note: Standing test does not apply in weightlessness. Pulseframe should compare with the in-flight baseline instead. This is a team note, not sourced. Threshold quote and source are in decisions.md section 3.

painScore in headache-co2
unit: 0-10
expected value or range in condition: Headache present; no numeric score given. Mostly tension-type in flight.
alert threshold: NOT FOUND (no numeric pain alert in any source read)
direction: high
inflight baseline ref: baselines-inflight.csv row 28
spaceflight adjustment: NOT FOUND
quote: Phenotypically, 170/189 (89.9%) episodes were tension-type headache (TTH) and 19/189 (10.1%) were migraine.

direction: high

respiratoryRate in headache-co2

quote: NOT FOUND

Protocol Choking or blocked airway (card choking-airway): tests
1. Can they speak or cough?: Ask: are you choking? Note yes if they can speak or cough hard.
2. Oxygen level after the airway is clear: Clip the pulse oximeter on a finger. Enter the oxygen level.
3. Pulse after the airway is clear: Read the pulse from the oximeter or count it for 1 minute. Enter the pulse.
4. Breathing rate after the airway is clear: Count breaths for 1 minute. Write down the number.

Protocol Choking or blocked airway (card choking-airway): immediate steps
1. Ask if they are choking: Ask: are you choking? Ask: can you speak? Look for hands at the throat.
2. If they can cough or speak, let them cough: Do not hit or squeeze them. Stay next to them. Act at once if the cough gets weak or they cannot speak.
3. If they cannot speak or breathe, call the crew: Shout for help. Start the next step now.

Protocol Choking or blocked airway (card choking-airway): immediate steps
4. Brace yourself behind them: Get behind the person. Hook your feet into a foot restraint or handrail. Wrap your arms around their waist.
5. Give thrusts: Make a fist. Put the thumb side just above the navel, well below the breastbone. Grab the fist with your other hand. Pull in and up fast. Repeat until the object comes out or they pass out.

Protocol Choking or blocked airway (card choking-airway): immediate steps
6. If they pass out, start CPR: Call every crew member. Restrain the person if you can. Start chest compressions. Look in the mouth before each breath. Remove an object only if you can see it and it is loose.
7. After the object comes out: Keep the person still. Check oxygen level and pulse. Send the case to the flight surgeon, even if they feel fine.

1. Pulse: Read the pulse. Enter it. Repeat every 5 minutes.

1. Fire or smoke: put on your mask first: Put on a protective mask now. Do not wait for air readings. Follow the station fire procedure.
2. Get the person out of the smoke: Move the person out of the affected module with the crew. Close the hatch as the fire procedure says. Keep a mask on the person.
3. If they are not breathing, start CPR: Check breathing and pulse. If there is none, start CPR now.

7. Electrical burn: cut the power first: Do not touch the person until the power is off. Then check pulse and breathing.
8. Cool the burn: Cool the burn with a wet gauze pad, a wet towel or a drink bag. Do not use ice.
9. Leave stuck clothing and blisters: Do not pull off clothing stuck to the burn. Do not break blisters.
10. Cover the burn: Cover the burn with a clean, dry dressing. Tape it loosely.

Protocol Headache in flight (including high CO2) (card headache-co2): tests
1. Danger sign check: Ask if the headache started suddenly and was explosive. Check for slurred speech, vision change, weak arms or legs, loss of balance or confusion. Note yes or no.
2. Pain score: Stay restrained. Enter a pain score from 0 to 10.
3. Body temperature: Take a temperature with the oral thermometer and enter it.

4. Systolic blood pressure: Stay restrained. Read systolic blood pressure on the monitor and enter it.
5. Diastolic blood pressure: Stay restrained. Read diastolic blood pressure on the monitor and enter it.
6. Heart rate: Read heart rate on the monitor and enter it.

Protocol Headache in flight (including high CO2) (card headache-co2): tests
7. Cabin CO2: Read the cabin CO2 value on the vehicle display or ask the ground. Write down the number and the unit. Ask crewmates if they have headaches too.

Protocol Headache in flight (including high CO2) (card headache-co2): immediate steps
1. Check for danger signs first: Do the danger sign check. If any answer is yes, call the flight surgeon now.
2. Check the cabin CO2: Read the CO2 value. Ask crewmates if they also have headaches.
3. Move to an area with good airflow: Move away from closed corners and sleep spots. Stay near moving air.
4. Rest and drink water: Stop hard work. Drink water.

Protocol Headache in flight (including high CO2) (card headache-co2): immediate steps
5. Measure and enter readings: Do the tests on this card. Enter each result.
6. Send the case to the flight surgeon: Continue to handoff and send the case. Include the CO2 value.

Space motion sickness: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Most likely in the first days of flight.

Protocol Space motion sickness: nausea and vomiting (card space-motion-sickness): tests
1. Sickness grade: Pick one grade. Mild: few symptoms, at most one vomit. Moderate: lasting symptoms, no more than 2 vomits. Severe: more than 2 vomits or cannot work.
2. Vomiting count: Count every time the person vomits. Write down the count and the time.
3. Heart rate: Stay restrained. Read heart rate on the blood pressure monitor and enter it.

Protocol Space motion sickness: nausea and vomiting (card space-motion-sickness): tests
4. Systolic blood pressure: Stay restrained. Read systolic blood pressure on the monitor and enter it.
5. Diastolic blood pressure: Stay restrained. Read diastolic blood pressure on the monitor and enter it.
6. Body temperature: Take a temperature with the oral thermometer and enter it.

Protocol Space motion sickness: nausea and vomiting (card space-motion-sickness): immediate steps
1. Restrain your body and keep your head still: Strap in or hold a rail. Keep your head still. Avoid nodding movements.
2. Close your eyes or focus on one task: Close your eyes. Or focus on one simple task.
3. Get away from smells and heat: Move away from strong smells. Move away from warm spots.
4. Sip fluids: Take small sips of water if you can keep them down.

Protocol Space motion sickness: nausea and vomiting (card space-motion-sickness): immediate steps
5. Count vomiting episodes: Record each vomit and the time.
6. Do not start an EVA or critical task: Tell the commander. Hold any spacewalk or critical task.
7. Send the case to the flight surgeon: Continue to handoff and send the case. The flight surgeon decides on treatment with you.

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 1. Doses
Question. The app refuses to show doses. In a real autonomous emergency the crew may need the labeled dose. What do onboard procedures and labels tell the crew, who authorizes, and what is the safest design?

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 1. Doses › What the sources say
The public ISS kit document is a contents list, not a dosing guide. Its columns are item, strength, route, quantity, unit, possible side effects, comments and location. Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 2. What the app may say when the ground is unreachable
Question. What do NASA and ESA procedures tell the crew to do when they cannot reach the ground?

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 2. What the app may say when the ground is unreachable › What the sources say
The 2001 ISS medical checklist puts the same note at the top of 31 procedures, including burns, cuts, motion sickness, eye problems and pain relief: begin treatment during loss of signal, then call the surgeon as soon as possible. This is the only explicit loss-of-signal rule we found. It is from 2001 and is historical.

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 2. What the app may say when the ground is unreachable › What the sources say
The same note says to contact the surgeon before giving any medicine marked with an asterisk. So in 2001 the starred medicines needed the ground, while first aid and the procedure steps did not.

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 2. What the app may say when the ground is unreachable › What the sources say
Emergency procedures in that checklist (choking, smoke inhalation, CPR) are written as steps the crew does at once, with no wait for the ground.

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 2. What the app may say when the ground is unreachable › What the sources say
Before a private medical conference, the checklist has the crew write down the symptoms, how long they have lasted, medicines taken and vital signs, and keep the checklist and kits within reach. That is a ready-made handoff packet.

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 2. What the app may say when the ground is unreachable › What the sources say
NASA operations have relied almost fully on real-time help from the ground. Delays or blackouts can stop that help, and a delay can reach 40 minutes. Sudden incapacitating events can quickly put a mission at risk. NASA says decision support tools are not yet robust enough.

Pulseframe product-safety decisions (section 9, items 1 to 6) › 2. What the app may say when the ground is unreachable › What the sources say
NOT FOUND: a current (post-2001) public ISS, Artemis or ESA rule for what crew may do without the ground; any ESA crew medical procedure. Looked in: OCHMO technical brief index, NASA-STD-3001 Appendix E, HRP 2017 evidence report, ESA web search, the public 2015 kit list.

Crew can take some mainly over-the-counter medicines without talking to the flight surgeon, so self-care is normal.
